Trump won 312 votes in the Electoral College, compared to his opponent Kamala Harris who received 226 votes in the electoral college. Former President [Donald Trump](/Donald_Trump_presidential_campaign,_2024 "Donald Trump presidential campaign, 2024") (R) won the November 5, 2024, presidential election. Trump won with 312 electoral votes, defeating Vice President [Kamala Harris](/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") (D) who received 226 electoral votes. This was the lowest electoral vote count received by a president running for re-election since 1916, when [Woodrow Wilson](/Woodrow_Wilson "Woodrow Wilson") (D) won re-election with 277 electoral votes.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Trump is also projected to win the popular vote.

This was the 60th presidential election in United States history, and the first held after the [2020 census](/Electoral_College_in_the_2024_presidential_election "Electoral College in the 2024 presidential election").[[2]](#cite_note-2) Trump was sworn into office on January 20, 2025, becoming the second president to ever serve two non-consecutive terms. The first to do so was [Grover Cleveland](/Grover_Cleveland "Grover Cleveland") (D), who held office from 1885 to 1889, and from 1893 to 1897.

Twenty-four candidates appeared on presidential election ballots across the country. Of those candidates, four qualified to appear on enough ballots — totaling at least 270 electoral votes — to win a majority of the Electoral College. Those [noteworthy presidential candidates](/Ballotpedia:Defining_noteworthy_presidential_candidates_(2024) "Ballotpedia:Defining noteworthy presidential candidates (2024)") were [Kamala Harris](/Kamala_Harris_presidential_campaign,_2024 "Kamala Harris presidential campaign, 2024") (D), [Donald Trump](/Donald_Trump_presidential_campaign,_2024 "Donald Trump presidential campaign, 2024") (R), [Jill Stein](/Jill_Stein "Jill Stein") (G), and [Chase Oliver](/Chase_Oliver_presidential_campaign,_2024 "Chase Oliver presidential campaign, 2024") (L).

# United States presidential election of 2024

![Britannica AI Icon](https://cdn.britannica.com/mendel-resources/3-196/images/chatbot/star-ai.svg?v=3.196.4)

### What was historically significant about [Republican](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Republican-Party) [Donald Trump](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Donald-Trump)’s 2024 election victory?

Trump became the first U.S. president to be elected to two nonconsecutive terms since [Grover Cleveland](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Grover-Cleveland) (1885–89 and 1893–97). He was also the first convicted felon to be elected president.

### Why did [Democrat](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Democratic-Party) [Joe Biden](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joe-Biden) withdraw from the 2024 presidential race?

Biden withdrew owing to pressure from Democrats concerned about his poor debate performance and his ability to defeat Donald Trump.

### What were the major themes of Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign?

The major themes of Trump’s campaign included criticism of Joe Biden’s economic management, opposition to government efforts to limit [climate change](https://www.britannica.com/science/climate-change), elimination of the “deep state,” and the [deportation](https://www.britannica.com/topic/deportation) of all undocumented immigrants.

### Who was the vice-presidential running mate of Democratic presidential nominee [Kamala Harris](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Kamala-Harris)?

Harris chose [Tim Walz](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Tim-Walz), the Democratic governor of Minnesota, as her vice-presidential running mate.

**United States presidential election of 2024**, American [election](https://www.britannica.com/topic/election-political-science), held on November 5, 2024, in which former [Republican](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Republican-Party) [president](https://www.britannica.com/topic/president-government-official) [Donald Trump](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Donald-Trump) (2017–21) defeated the Democratic nominee, Vice Pres. [Kamala Harris](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Kamala-Harris). Trump, who lost his bid for reelection in 2020 to Democrat [Joe Biden](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joe-Biden), is the first U.S. president to be elected to two nonconsecutive terms since [Grover Cleveland](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Grover-Cleveland), the 22nd and 24th president of the United States (1885–89 and 1893–97). Having been convicted of a felony crime in May 2024, Trump also became the first convicted felon to be elected president upon his sentencing without punishment in January 2025 (*see below* [Background: Trump’s indictments and trials](https://www.britannica.com/event/United-States-presidential-election-of-2024#ref359374)). At age 78, Trump is the oldest person to win the office. Trump won the popular vote by a relatively small margin but earned a sizeable majority of electors, or members of the [Electoral College](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Electoral-College-United-States), whose vote in December confirmed his election. Trump’s victory marks one of the most stunning political comebacks in U.S. history.

In June 2024, while campaigning for his own second term, Pres. Biden performed poorly in a nationally televised debate with Trump. Under intense pressure from prominent Democrats who feared he would lose the election, Biden withdrew his candidacy and [endorsed](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/endorsed) Harris as his replacement. In early August, Harris was officially named the Democratic Party’s presidential nominee following her victory in a virtual vote of party delegates.

## Background: Trump’s indictments and trials

![On the campaign trail](https://cdn.britannica.com/81/259781-050-0ED3BC3D/President-Joe-Biden-Vice-President-Kamala-Harris-campaign-rally-Girard-College-Phildelphia-PA-May-2024.jpg?w=300)

Soon after the [U.S. congressional](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Congress-of-the-United-States) midterm elections in November 2022, Trump announced his candidacy for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, and he subsequently remained by far the most popular presidential candidate among Republican voters. In 2023 Trump was indicted on multiple state and federal criminal charges, including acts of business fraud designed to conceal [a hush-money payment to the adult-film star](https://www.britannica.com/biography/New-York-indictment-of-Donald-Trump-2229245) Stormy Daniels; [Trump’s removal and concealment of classified documents from the White House](https://www.britannica.com/biography/federal-indictment-of-Donald-J-Trump-documents-case-2226364) upon leaving office; and [his various efforts to overturn the presidential election of 2020](https://www.britannica.com/biography/federal-indictment-of-Donald-Trump-2020-election-and-January-6-attack-2228782).

![Donald Trump](https://cdn.britannica.com/18/273318-050-9DE2F788/President-Donald-J-Trump-portrait-2025.jpg)

Trump’s attempts to prevent or reverse Biden’s victory in the [2020 election](https://www.britannica.com/event/United-States-presidential-election-of-2020), according to federal and state indictments, included his participation in a [conspiracy](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/conspiracy) to create fraudulent slates of pro-Trump electors in certain swing states, his pressuring of Georgia’s secretary of state to “find” enough votes to belatedly declare Trump the victor in that state’s election, and his pressuring of Vice Pres. Mike Pence, who presided over Congress’s ceremonial counting of electoral votes on January 6, 2021, to alter the official electoral vote count.) In addition, Trump and his private conglomerate, the Trump Organization, were found liable on civil charges of business fraud in a suit filed by the [New York](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-state) attorney general’s office, and Trump himself was found [liable](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/liable) on civil charges of [sexual abuse](https://www.britannica.com/topic/sexual-abuse) and [defamation](https://www.britannica.com/topic/defamation) in two suits filed by the writer E. Jean Carroll. In February 2024, the judge in the business fraud suit ordered Trump to pay more than $350 million in penalties and barred him from serving as an officer or director of any company in New York state, including the Trump Organization, for three years.

The ensuing trials in Trump’s three criminal cases were originally scheduled to begin in March and May 2024, at the height of the primary season, making it likely at the time that Trump would need to limit or at least coordinate his campaign events to accommodate his appearances in court. In each case, however, Trump’s legal team continuously filed motions and appeals designed to delay the trial’s starting date or dismiss the charges altogether.

In January 2024 the federal criminal case concerning Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election, whose trial date had been scheduled for March 4, was indefinitely delayed after Trump appealed the district court’s ruling rejecting his [contention](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/contention) that he should be immune from prosecution for acts he committed while serving as president. In February a three-judge panel of the Court of Appeals for the [District of Columbia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Washington-DC) Circuit agreed with the district court that Trump did not possess absolute, or permanent, immunity and thus could be prosecuted as a private citizen for his criminal acts as president. Trump then asked the [U.S. Supreme Court](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Supreme-Court-of-the-United-States) to put the panel’s ruling on hold while he filed a petition for review by the full appeals court. The Supreme Court instead chose to hear the case itself, scheduling oral arguments for April 2024. The Court’s response officially extended the delay of Trump’s criminal trial until after “the sending down of the judgment of this Court,” which did not take place until the end of the Court’s 2023–24 term in July. (*See* [indictments of Donald Trump](https://www.britannica.com/biography/indictments-of-Donald-Trump-2229401).).

The Court’s decision in the case, [*Trump* v. *United States*](https://www.britannica.com/topic/major-Supreme-Court-cases-from-the-2023-24-term-2232860#ref379330), held that former presidents are entitled to absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for actions that involve the exercise of their “core [constitutional](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/constitutional) powers” and to “presumptive immunity” for all other official acts. (Citing the 1982 Supreme Court decision in *Nixon* v. *Fitzgerald*, the Court explained that an official act for which the president is presumptively immune can be prosecuted only if “the Government can show that applying a criminal prohibition to that act would pose no ‘dangers of intrusion on the authority and functions of the Executive Branch.’”) The Court did not provide a specific definition of an official presidential act but instead offered a set of principles and observations for use by the district court, to which it remanded the case to determine which of the acts for which Trump was being prosecuted qualified as official. # US presidential election results 2024

## Presidential results map

This map of the US states was filled in as presidential results were called. It shows huge swathes of the country coloured red for Republicans including much of the south, mid and north west regions. Kamala Harris picked up states in the north east, the west coast, as well as Colorado, New Mexico, Illinois and Minnesota, all coloured in blue. Donald Trump passed the critical threshold of 270 electoral college votes with a projected win in the state of Wisconsin making him the next US president.

## Congress

Voters are also choosing new members of Congress who play a key part in passing laws that can have a profound effect on American life.

## Senate, House and governors

Thirty-four seats were contested in the Senate, the upper chamber in Congress. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, are being voted on. Voters in 11 states also elected a governor.
